sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 102 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: A prayer of the afflicted
study.intro: Psalm 102 is the prayer of someone worn down by suffering who pours out a lament before the LORD. The first half describes fading days, sleepless nights and loneliness. Then the psalm turns to God, enthroned forever, who will rebuild Zion and hear the destitute. It ends by contrasting our brief lives with God's unending years, a passage Hebrews applies to Jesus.
study.context: Psalm 102 has a unique heading: it names no author but describes the person praying, 'one who is afflicted, when he grows faint.' It is one of the seven traditional penitential psalms. Its references to Zion's stones and dust suggest the ruins of Jerusalem during or after the exile. Verses 25-27 are quoted in Hebrews 1:10-12 as words addressed to the Son, showing that the unchanging Lord of this psalm is revealed in Jesus.
study.peopleNote: No author is named; the heading describes any afflicted person who grows faint, which invites every sufferer to pray these words. Jesus is linked because Hebrews 1:10-12 applies verses 25-27 to Him as the eternal Creator. God is never portrayed as a human body in planned art.

verses.title: A cry that reaches God
verses.heading: Let my cry come before You
verses.meaning: The heading describes the speaker as 'one who is afflicted, when he grows faint and pours out his lament before the LORD.' Then he prays, 'Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry for help come before You.' This psalm was written to be borrowed by anyone at the end of their strength. Before the details of his pain, he asks for one thing: that his cry would truly reach God.
verses.context: Psalm 62:8 urges, 'Pour out your hearts before Him.' Hannah poured out her soul before the LORD in 1 Samuel 1:15. Lamentations 2:19 calls Jerusalem to pour out her heart like water before the Lord.
explore: Lament
A prayer that honestly brings grief, pain or complaint to God while still trusting Him to listen.
Grows faint
Becomes weak and worn out in body or spirit, unable to keep going in one's own strength.
verses.reflect: What would it look like for you to pour out your heart honestly before God today?
verses.alt: A tired woman kneels on a stone floor at dusk with open hands.

verses.title: Do not hide Your face
verses.heading: Answer me quickly
verses.meaning: Verse 2 pleads, 'Do not hide Your face from me in my day of distress. Incline Your ear to me; answer me quickly when I call.' To see God's face meant knowing His favor and nearness; to have it hidden felt like abandonment. The psalmist asks God to bend down and listen, the way someone leans close to hear a weak voice. His urgency is honest: he cannot wait long.
verses.context: Numbers 6:25 blesses, 'May the LORD cause His face to shine upon you.' Psalm 13:1 asks, 'How long will You hide Your face from me?' Psalm 69:17 also prays, 'Hide not Your face from Your servant.'
explore: Hide Your face
A picture of God seeming distant or withholding His favor, felt as deep loneliness.
Incline Your ear
Bend down to listen closely, an image of God's attentive care for the weak.
verses.reflect: When God feels far away, what helps you keep speaking to Him?
verses.alt: A lone figure stands in a dark courtyard looking up toward a faint light.

verses.title: Smoke and embers
verses.heading: My days vanish like smoke
verses.meaning: Verse 3 says, 'For my days vanish like smoke, and my bones burn like glowing embers.' Smoke rises and is gone in moments, and the psalmist feels his life slipping away just as fast. His bones burn like coals, perhaps describing fever or the deep inner ache of grief. Suffering often affects body and soul together, and Scripture gives words for both.
verses.context: James 4:14 says, 'You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.' Job 30:30 describes his bones burning with fever. Psalm 31:10 says, 'My life is consumed with grief.'
explore: Smoke
A picture of something that disappears quickly and cannot be held, like a short life.
Glowing embers
Hot coals that burn slowly, picturing pain that smolders deep within the body.
verses.reflect: How does knowing your life is brief change what you want to spend it on?
verses.alt: Thin smoke drifts upward from a small clay hearth with glowing coals.

verses.title: Withered like grass
verses.heading: I forget to eat my bread
verses.meaning: Verse 4 confesses, 'My heart is afflicted, and withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread.' Grass in the dry season turns brown and brittle under the sun. The psalmist's heart feels that drained. Grief can steal even the desire to eat. The Bible does not shame this weakness; it names it honestly and brings it before God.
verses.context: Hannah wept and would not eat in 1 Samuel 1:7. Elijah, exhausted, was fed by an angel in 1 Kings 19:5-7. Isaiah 40:7 says, 'The grass withers... when the breath of the LORD blows on it.'
explore: Afflicted
Struck down or deeply troubled, bearing a weight of pain that presses on the heart.
Withered
Dried up and lifeless, like plants scorched by heat and lacking water.
verses.reflect: Is there a practical way you need to care for your body during a hard season?
verses.alt: A field of dry, browned grass under a hot pale sky.

verses.title: Skin and bones
verses.heading: My loud groaning
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says, 'Through my loud groaning my skin hangs on my bones.' Long sorrow has left the psalmist thin and worn. His groaning is loud, not polite or hidden. God's people are allowed to groan. Romans 8 even says the Spirit intercedes for us with groans too deep for words, so our groaning is never wasted before God.
verses.context: Romans 8:26 says the Spirit intercedes 'with groans too deep for words.' Exodus 2:24 says God heard Israel's groaning in Egypt. Job 19:20 says, 'My skin and flesh cling to my bones.'
explore: Groaning
Deep sounds of pain or longing that come when words are not enough.
Hangs on my bones
A picture of becoming so thin from suffering that the body looks wasted.
verses.reflect: What groaning in your life do you need to trust God with, even without words?
verses.alt: A thin man sits wrapped in a blanket on a mat, head bowed.

verses.title: Owl among the ruins
verses.heading: Like a desert owl
verses.meaning: Verse 6 says, 'I am like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins.' Owls lived in abandoned places, crying out at night among broken walls. The psalmist feels just as isolated, like a creature in a deserted city. The image fits the ruins of Jerusalem mentioned later. Loneliness can feel like living among rubble where no one comes.
verses.context: Isaiah 34:11 pictures owls dwelling in a ruined land. Zephaniah 2:14 describes owls in the ruins of Nineveh. Job 30:29 says, 'I have become a brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches.'
explore: Desert owl
A bird of lonely wilderness places, often a symbol of desolation in Scripture.
Ruins
Broken buildings left empty after destruction, a picture of loss and abandonment.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel most isolated right now, and who could you invite into it?
verses.alt: A small owl perched on a crumbling stone wall under moonlight.

verses.title: A lone bird
verses.heading: I lie awake
verses.meaning: Verse 7 says, 'I lie awake; I am like a lone bird on a housetop.' Sleep will not come, and he feels like a single bird sitting on a flat roof while everyone below sleeps. Sleeplessness magnifies loneliness. Yet even this lonely bird is in God's sight; Jesus said not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father.
verses.context: Matthew 10:29 says not one sparrow falls apart from the Father. Psalm 77:4 says, 'You have kept my eyes from closing.' Psalm 4:8 shows the peace of lying down in safety.
explore: Lie awake
To be unable to sleep, often from worry, grief or pain that fills the night.
Housetop
The flat roof of an ancient home, used for sleeping, drying crops and prayer.
verses.reflect: What do you do with long, sleepless nights? Could they become times of prayer?
verses.alt: A single small bird sits on a flat mud-brick rooftop at night.

verses.title: Taunted all day
verses.heading: My enemies ridicule me
verses.meaning: Verse 8 says, 'All day long my enemies taunt me; they ridicule me and curse me.' On top of illness and loneliness come mockers. They use his suffering as a reason to scorn him, even turning his name into a curse. Jesus also endured mocking in His suffering, so He understands this pain from the inside.
verses.context: Matthew 27:39-41 records people mocking Jesus on the cross. Psalm 42:10 says enemies taunt, 'Where is your God?' 1 Peter 2:23 says Jesus did not retaliate when insulted.
explore: Taunt
To mock someone cruelly, often by pointing out their weakness or trouble.
Curse
To call down harm on someone, or use their name as an example of ruin.
verses.reflect: How can you respond to ridicule the way Jesus did, entrusting yourself to God?
verses.alt: Two people point and laugh at a distance while a man walks away alone.

verses.title: Ashes for bread
verses.heading: Mixed my drink with tears
verses.meaning: Verse 9 says, 'For I have eaten ashes like bread and mixed my drink with tears.' Mourners in Israel sat in ashes and put them on their heads. The psalmist says sorrow has become his daily food. Tears fall into his cup. It is a vivid way of saying that grief has soaked into every ordinary part of his day.
verses.context: Job 2:8 shows Job sitting among the ashes. Psalm 42:3 says, 'My tears have been my food both day and night.' Isaiah 61:3 promises 'a crown of beauty for ashes.'
explore: Ashes
A sign of deep mourning and humility, worn or sat in during grief or repentance.
Tears in the cup
A picture of sorrow mixing into every meal, so that daily life tastes of grief.
verses.reflect: Isaiah promises beauty for ashes. Where do you long for God to make that exchange?
verses.alt: A plain clay cup and a small loaf beside a scattering of grey ash.

verses.title: Cast aside
verses.heading: Your indignation and wrath
verses.meaning: Verse 10 continues, 'because of Your indignation and wrath, for You have picked me up and cast me aside.' The psalmist senses that his suffering is connected to God's anger, perhaps against sin, perhaps against the nation in exile. He feels lifted up and then thrown down. Yet he keeps praying to the very God he feels has cast him off.
verses.context: Lamentations 3:31-33 says the Lord will not cast off forever and does not willingly afflict. Hebrews 12:6 says the Lord disciplines those He loves. Psalm 30:5 says His anger is for a moment.
explore: Indignation
Strong, righteous displeasure at wrong, here felt as God's anger against sin.
Cast aside
Thrown away like something unwanted, a feeling of being rejected by God.
verses.reflect: When you feel set aside by God, what truths can keep you turning back to Him?
verses.alt: A broken clay jar lies on rocky ground beside a path.

verses.title: Evening shadows
verses.heading: My days lengthen like shadows
verses.meaning: Verse 11 says, 'My days are like lengthening shadows, and I wither away like grass.' Late in the afternoon shadows stretch long before the sun sets and darkness comes. The psalmist feels his life nearing its evening. He repeats the withering grass image from verse 4. This is the low point of the psalm, just before everything turns.
verses.context: Job 14:2 says man is 'like a fleeting shadow' that 'does not endure.' Psalm 109:23 says, 'I fade away like a lengthening shadow.' 1 Peter 1:24 says all flesh is like grass.
explore: Lengthening shadows
Shadows that stretch out late in the day, signaling that night is near.
Wither away
To fade slowly and lose strength, like grass drying up in the heat.
verses.reflect: How does facing the shortness of life make you value God's eternal nature more?
verses.alt: Long evening shadows stretch from olive trees across a quiet hillside.

verses.title: But You remain enthroned
verses.heading: Your renown endures
verses.meaning: Verse 12 turns everything: 'But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever; Your renown endures to all generations.' After eleven verses about his fading life, the psalmist looks up. He is passing, but God is not. God's throne does not wobble, and His fame outlasts every generation. Hope begins when we shift our eyes from our weakness to God's permanence.
verses.context: Lamentations 5:19 says, 'You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation.' Psalm 9:7 says the LORD abides forever. Exodus 3:15 says His name is remembered from generation to generation.
explore: Enthroned
Seated as King with full authority, a picture of God's unshaken rule.
Renown
Fame and reputation; the remembrance of who God is and what He has done.
verses.reflect: What changes in your outlook when you say, 'But You, O LORD'?
verses.alt: Morning light breaks over distant hills after a long night.

verses.title: The appointed time
verses.heading: Compassion on Zion
verses.meaning: Verse 13 declares, 'You will rise up and have compassion on Zion, for it is time to show her favor—the appointed time has come.' The psalmist moves from his own pain to the city of God. He trusts that God has set a time for restoration. God's mercy is not random; it arrives on His schedule, which is never too late.
verses.context: Daniel 9:2 shows Daniel learning from Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years. Isaiah 40:1-2 announces comfort for Jerusalem. Galatians 4:4 says God sent His Son 'when the time had fully come.'
explore: Zion
The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood, often standing for God's people.
Appointed time
A moment God has set in advance for His purposes to be fulfilled.
verses.reflect: What are you waiting on God for, and how can you trust His timing?
verses.alt: A ruined city wall with new green shoots growing between the stones.

verses.title: Love for the dust
verses.heading: Delight in her stones
verses.meaning: Verse 14 explains, 'For Your servants delight in her stones and take pity on her dust.' Jerusalem lies in rubble, yet God's people still cherish even its broken stones. Their love for the ruined city mirrors God's own heart. Nehemiah later wept over these same walls and then led the people to rebuild them.
verses.context: Nehemiah 1:3-4 shows Nehemiah weeping over Jerusalem's broken walls. Nehemiah 2:17 says, 'Let us rebuild the wall.' Psalm 137:5-6 shows exiles who refuse to forget Jerusalem.
explore: Stones
The building blocks of the ruined city, still loved by those who long for its renewal.
Take pity
To feel tender compassion, here even for the dust of a destroyed place.
verses.reflect: What broken place or community has God given you a burden to care for?
verses.alt: Hands gently lifting a cut stone from a pile of rubble.

verses.title: Nations will fear
verses.heading: Kings will fear Your glory
verses.meaning: Verse 15 says, 'So the nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear Your glory.' When God restores His people, the whole world will notice. His rescue of one small nation becomes a display of His glory to every king. God's care for His people always has the wider world in view.
verses.context: Isaiah 60:3 says nations will come to your light. Psalm 67:7 says all the ends of the earth will fear Him. Ezekiel 36:23 says the nations will know that He is the LORD.
explore: Fear the name
To honor and revere God, recognizing His power and holiness.
Glory
The visible weight and splendor of who God is, displayed in His works.
verses.reflect: How might God use His work in your life to show others who He is?
verses.alt: Distant city gates with travelers from many lands approaching.

verses.title: Zion rebuilt
verses.heading: He has appeared in His glory
verses.meaning: Verse 16 says, 'For the LORD will rebuild Zion; He has appeared in His glory.' The psalmist speaks of the rebuilding as so certain that God's glory is already seen. Restoration is God's work, not merely human effort. When God rebuilds what was broken, the result shows His splendor, not ours, and everyone can see it.
verses.context: Psalm 127:1 says unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Psalm 147:2 says the LORD builds up Jerusalem. Ezra 6:14-15 records the temple's completion.
explore: Rebuild
To restore what was destroyed, here the city and life of God's people.
Appeared
Made Himself known; God's glory shown openly through His saving acts.
verses.reflect: What has God rebuilt in your life that now displays His goodness?
verses.alt: Workers set fresh stones on a city wall under bright sunlight.

verses.title: Prayers of the destitute
verses.heading: He will not despise them
verses.meaning: Verse 17 promises, 'He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer.' The destitute are those stripped of everything. Human rulers often ignore them, but God turns toward them. This is the answer to verse 1: the afflicted person who cried out is exactly the kind of person God hears.
verses.context: Psalm 22:24 says God has not despised the affliction of the afflicted. Psalm 51:17 says a broken heart He will not despise. Luke 18:13-14 shows God justifying the humble tax collector.
explore: Destitute
Utterly poor and without help, having lost everything that once supported them.
Despise
To look down on as worthless; God refuses to treat the needy this way.
verses.reflect: Do you believe God takes your weakest, most desperate prayers seriously?
verses.alt: A poor woman in a head cloth prays by a doorway in soft light.

verses.title: Written for the future
verses.heading: A people not yet created
verses.meaning: Verse 18 says, 'Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD.' The psalmist wants God's rescue recorded so future believers will praise Him. That includes us. When we read this psalm, we are the people not yet created who are now praising God for His faithfulness.
verses.context: Romans 15:4 says what was written in the past was written to teach us. Psalm 78:4 says, 'We will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD.' Psalm 22:31 speaks of a people yet unborn.
explore: Generation to come
Future people who will hear of God's works and learn to trust Him.
Not yet created
People not yet born, whom God already has in view as future worshipers.
verses.reflect: What story of God's faithfulness should you write down for those who come after you?
verses.alt: An open scroll and reed pen on a wooden table by a window.

verses.title: Looking down from heaven
verses.heading: The LORD gazed out
verses.meaning: Verse 19 says, 'For He looked down from the heights of His sanctuary; the LORD gazed out from heaven to earth.' God's high throne does not make Him distant. From heaven He looks carefully at the earth. His exaltation and His attention go together. The highest King is also the one who sees the lowest places.
verses.context: Isaiah 57:15 says the high and lofty One dwells with the contrite and lowly. Exodus 3:7 says, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people.' Psalm 33:13 says the LORD looks down from heaven.
explore: Sanctuary
God's holy dwelling place, here His heavenly throne room.
Gazed
Looked with steady, careful attention rather than a passing glance.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God sees you clearly from His throne?
verses.alt: Light streaming down through clouds onto a small village below.

verses.title: Setting prisoners free
verses.heading: A prisoner's groaning
verses.meaning: Verse 20 says God looks down 'to hear a prisoner's groaning, to release those condemned to death.' Exiles, captives and the condemned are precisely the ones God listens to. He hears groans that no one else hears. Jesus announced that He came to proclaim freedom to captives, fulfilling this heart of God.
verses.context: Luke 4:18 says Jesus came 'to proclaim liberty to the captives.' Psalm 79:11 prays, 'May the groans of the captives reach You.' Psalm 146:7 says the LORD sets prisoners free.
explore: Prisoner
Someone held captive, here possibly exiles in a foreign land or those bound by sin.
Condemned to death
Those under a death sentence, whom God has power to release.
verses.reflect: Who do you know who feels trapped, and how can you pray for their freedom?
verses.alt: An opened prison door with light pouring into a stone cell.

verses.title: Praise in Jerusalem
verses.heading: Proclaim His name in Zion
verses.meaning: Verse 21 gives the purpose of rescue: 'that they may proclaim the name of the LORD in Zion and praise Him in Jerusalem.' The freed prisoners do not simply go home; they go to worship. God saves people so that they will declare His name. Rescue leads to praise, and praise spreads the knowledge of God.
verses.context: Psalm 107:2 says, 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so.' Exodus 8:1 says, 'Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.' 1 Peter 2:9 says we are called to proclaim His virtues.
explore: Proclaim
To announce publicly, telling others what God is like and what He has done.
Jerusalem
The city of God's temple, the center of Israel's worship.
verses.reflect: How can you proclaim what God has done for you this week?
verses.alt: A crowd gathering with raised hands outside a city gate at sunrise.

verses.title: Kingdoms gathered
verses.heading: Peoples serve the LORD
verses.meaning: Verse 22 completes the picture: 'when peoples and kingdoms assemble to serve the LORD.' The vision expands beyond Israel to whole nations coming to worship. What began as one person's lonely cry ends with the world gathered before God. Christians see this pointing ahead to the gospel going to every nation through Jesus Christ.
verses.context: Isaiah 2:2-3 says many peoples will stream to the mountain of the LORD. Revelation 7:9 shows a multitude from every nation before the throne. Zechariah 8:22 says many peoples will seek the LORD in Jerusalem.
explore: Assemble
To come together in one place, here for the shared purpose of worship.
Serve the LORD
To worship and obey God, giving Him loyalty and honor.
verses.reflect: How does the vision of every nation worshiping God encourage you today?
verses.alt: People in varied clothing walk together along a road toward a hill city.

verses.title: Strength broken on the road
verses.heading: He has cut short my days
verses.meaning: Verse 23 returns to personal pain: 'He has broken my strength on the way; He has cut short my days.' The psalmist has seen the big hope, yet his own body is still failing. Faith does not erase present weakness. Halfway through life's journey, his strength gives out, and he honestly admits it to God in prayer.
verses.context: 2 Corinthians 4:16 says outwardly we are wasting away, yet inwardly renewed. Isaiah 38:10 records Hezekiah fearing death in the middle of his days. Job 17:1 says, 'My days are extinguished.'
explore: On the way
In the middle of life's journey, before the expected end.
Cut short
Shortened before its natural length, like a thread snipped early.
verses.reflect: How do you hold God's great promises together with your present weaknesses?
verses.alt: A walking staff lying across a dusty road at midday.

verses.title: Not in the midst of my days
verses.heading: Your years go on
verses.meaning: Verse 24 prays, 'I say: “O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days! Your years go on through all generations.' The psalmist asks God not to end his life early. He sets his short years beside God's endless ones. The contrast is not cold; it is a reason to ask. The eternal God has plenty of time to give.
verses.context: Isaiah 38:5 records God adding fifteen years to Hezekiah's life. Psalm 90:10 numbers our days at seventy or eighty years. Psalm 90:2 says from everlasting to everlasting You are God.
explore: In the midst of my days
In the middle of life, before old age, when death feels too soon.
Through all generations
Without end, outlasting every human lifetime and every age.
verses.reflect: Is it right to ask God for more time? What would you do with it?
verses.alt: An old man and a young boy sit together on a stone bench at sunset.

verses.title: Foundations of the earth
verses.heading: The work of Your hands
verses.meaning: Verse 25 says, 'In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands.' The psalmist looks back to creation. God existed before the world and built it like a craftsman. Hebrews 1:10 applies these words to the Son, declaring that Jesus is the Creator of all things.
verses.contextTitle: The Creator revealed in the Son
verses.context: Hebrews 1:10 quotes this verse about the Son. John 1:3 says through Him all things were made. Genesis 1:1 says, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.'
explore: Foundations
The base on which something is built, a picture of God firmly establishing the earth.
Work of Your hands
What God has personally made, showing His skill and ownership.
verses.reflect: How does knowing Jesus made the world deepen your trust in Him?
verses.alt: Mountains and a starry sky stretch over a wide, quiet valley.

verses.title: Worn out like a garment
verses.heading: Like clothing You will change them
verses.meaning: Verse 26 says, 'They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. Like clothing You will change them, and they will be passed on.' Even earth and sky are not permanent. Like an old robe they will wear thin, and God will exchange them for new ones. Only the Maker remains unchanged.
verses.context: Isaiah 51:6 says the heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth wear out like a garment. 2 Peter 3:13 looks for new heavens and a new earth. Revelation 21:1 shows the first heaven and earth passing away.
explore: Perish
To come to an end; even the created world is not eternal.
Change them
To replace like clothing, a picture of God renewing creation in the end.
verses.reflect: What are you treating as permanent that is actually passing away?
verses.alt: A worn, faded cloak folded beside a new woven garment.

verses.title: You remain the same
verses.heading: Your years will never end
verses.meaning: Verse 27 declares, 'But You remain the same, and Your years will never end.' This is the anchor of the whole psalm. Our days vanish like smoke, but God does not change. Hebrews 13:8 echoes this: 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.' What He promised, He still means, and always will.
verses.context: Hebrews 1:12 applies this to the Son. Hebrews 13:8 says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever. Malachi 3:6 says, 'I, the LORD, do not change.'
explore: The same
Unchanging in character, purpose and faithfulness across all time.
Never end
Without limit or ending; God's life has no final day and no decline.
verses.reflect: Which part of God's unchanging character do you need to rest in today?
verses.alt: An ancient rock outcrop stands firm while clouds move swiftly past.

verses.title: Children dwell securely
verses.heading: Descendants established before You
verses.meaning: Verse 28 ends, 'The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You.' The psalmist may not live long, but God's people will continue. Because God endures, His promises reach the next generation. The psalm that began with one dying voice ends with a future full of children safe in God's presence.
verses.context: Psalm 103:17 says His loving devotion is on those who fear Him, and His righteousness on children's children. Isaiah 59:21 promises God's words will not depart from your descendants. Acts 2:39 says the promise is for you and your children.
explore: Dwell securely
Live in safety and stability, without fear of being uprooted.
Established
Made firm and lasting, set in place by God Himself.
verses.reflect: How can you help the next generation know the faithful God of this psalm?
verses.alt: Children play in a sunny courtyard while parents watch from a doorway.
